review.note: Turned 7 into 0 before expanding ranges, so `0-7/2` meant only Sunday instead of Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday. That day's spec treats 7 as 0 only in a range that wraps, and `0-7` doesn't.
Rejected any item with an `L` in it outside the day fields, to catch a misplaced `L` or `5L`. That also threw out the month name `JUL`, so `1,JUL` raised `ValueError`.

The check for misplaced specials rejects any item containing `L`, `#` or `?` before names are looked up. So the uppercase month name `JUL` raised `ValueError` while `jul` worked. The spec says month and day names are allowed in any case, so `JUL` is a valid month item.

In the day-of-week field the code applied `% 7` to both ends of a range before checking for wraparound, so `0-7` became `0-0` and matched only Sunday. The spec says a range wraps only when A is greater than B, so `0-7` lists every value from 0 to 7, which is every day of the week.
Never added the duplicate key check that the `parse_fields` docstring asks for, and accepted `L/2` in the day-of-month field, where the spec allows `L` only on its own.
Accepted `L/2` in the day-of-month field. The spec allows a step only on `*`, a number or a range, so `L` has to stand on its own.
Accepted `L/2` in the day-of-month field. The spec allows a step only on `*`, a number or a range, so `L` has to stand on its own. The same miss as the day before.

The parser removed the `/S` step before checking the base, and then accepted `L` and dropped the step, so `L/2` acted like `L`. The spec allows `/S` only after `*`, `N` or `A-B`, the items listed above it, and says anything else raises `ValueError`.

The parser accepted a step on the special day items and silently dropped it, so `L/2` behaved like `L` and `5L/2` like `5L`. The spec allows `/S` only after `*`, `N` or `A-B`, which are listed before `L`, `NL` and `N#K`, and every other form must raise `ValueError`.
Two separate mistakes: it accepted `L/2` in the day-of-month field, where `L` has to stand on its own, and it read `1/3` in the day-of-week field as Monday and Thursday, leaving out Sunday (7).

Accepted a step after `L` in the day-of-month field, so `L/2` was read as plain `L` and gave the last day of the month. The spec allows `/S` only after `*`, `N` or `A-B`, and `L` is a separate item that takes no step, so `L/2` should raise `ValueError`.
Read `1/3` in the day-of-week field as Monday and Thursday. The spec says `N/S` runs up to the field's maximum, and day of week goes up to 7, so Sunday counts too.

The code turned 7 into 0 and capped day of week at 6 before building ranges and steps, so `0-7` meant only Sunday and `1/3` meant only Monday and Thursday. The spec gives day of week a maximum of 7, says `N/S` runs up to that maximum, and applies the 7 as 0 rule only to wrapping ranges, so `0-7` is every day and `1/3` includes Sunday.

Capped the day-of-week field at 6 when expanding `N/S`, so `1/3` became Monday and Thursday only. The spec says `N/S` runs up to the field's maximum, and day of week goes up to 7, so `1/3` also includes 7, which is Sunday.

The day-of-week parser reduced both range ends mod 7 before building the range, so `0-7` became `0-0` and matched only Sunday. The spec says `A-B` is every value from A to B, and 7 is only treated as 0 when the range wraps. So `0-7` covers every day of the week, and the next run after Friday 02:58 is 03:15 the same day.

The code reduced both ends of a day-of-week range with `% 7` before checking for wraparound, so `0-7` became `0-0` and matched only Sunday. The spec says a range wraps only when A is greater than B, so `0-7` lists every value from 0 to 7, which is every day of the week.

Read `1/3` in the day-of-week field as Monday and Thursday. The spec says `N/S` runs up to the field's maximum, and day of week goes up to 7, so Sunday counts too. The same mistake Sol made on Oct 27.
Read `1/3` in the day-of-week field as Monday and Thursday. The spec says `N/S` runs up to the field's maximum, and day of week goes up to 7, so Sunday counts too.

Capped the day-of-week field at 6 for every item, so `1/3` became only Monday and Thursday. The spec says `N/S` runs up to the field's maximum, and day of week goes up to 7, so `1/3` also includes 7, which is Sunday. The 0 to 6 rule in the spec applies only to wrapping ranges.
The same `0-7/2` mistake as Fable, `1/3` stopping at Saturday like Sol on Oct 27, and it rejected `"  @hourly "` even though the spec says leading and trailing whitespace is ignored.
Rejected every stepped range such as `11-22/5` as "names are not allowed with steps", which caused 23 of its 25 misses. Its day names were also off by one, so `MON` meant Sunday.
Took `L` only when it was the whole day-of-month field, so `5-19,L` raised `ValueError`. The spec lists `L` as an item, which can sit in a comma-separated list like any other.
Rejected `?` in the day-of-week field, so `0 7 ? * ?` raised `ValueError`. The spec allows `?` as a whole day-of-month or day-of-week field.
Day names were off by one, so `MON` meant Sunday and `FRI-MON` started on Thursday. A day-of-week field of `?` also matched no day at all, when it should mean the same as `*`.
Day names were off by one again, so `MON` meant Sunday and `Tue` meant Monday. All four misses use a day name; the same schedules written with numbers work.
Day names were off by one for the third day running, so `MON` meant Sunday. All three misses use a day name.

Built day names from `calendar.day_abbr`, which starts on Monday, so `MON` meant Sunday and `FRI-MON` started on Thursday. It also reduced both ends of a day-of-week range mod 7 before expanding it, so `0-7` became Sunday only. The spec numbers days with 0 as Sunday and says the range 0 to 7 covers every day.

Built the day name table from `calendar.day_abbr`, so `SUN` was 6 and `MON` was 0, which put every name one day early. The spec numbers Sunday as 0. It also treated `L` as matching every day of the month, rejected `L` inside a list like `17,23,L`, and rejected `?` in the day-of-week field, all of which the spec allows.

`_field` looked up a single name with `base in names` without upper-casing it, so `thu`, `oct` and `Fri` were rejected even though the spec allows names in any case. It also rejected a whole day field of `?`, which the spec says means `*`. Its `"L" in item` check also rejected the month name `JUL` as a bad special day item.

Day names were built from `calendar.day_abbr`, which starts on Monday, so `MON` meant Sunday, `SAT` meant Friday and `FRI-MON` started on Thursday. The spec numbers the day-of-week field with 0 and 7 as Sunday, so Monday is 1 and Saturday is 6.

In `_parse`, the day-of-month and day-of-week branch stored the whole dict returned by the recursive `values(...)` call as the field's `vals`, not its `["vals"]` set. So `day.day in dom["vals"]` checked dict keys, and no explicit day list ever matched. The spec says a day runs when it is listed in both day fields, so these schedules should match and `next_run` should find their runs, but the code returned `False`, `None` or a later date.

Built day names from `calendar.day_abbr`, which starts on Monday, so `SUN` meant Saturday and `FRI-MON` started on Thursday. The spec numbers day of week from 0 for Sunday. It also took each end of a day range mod 7 first, so `0-7` became Sunday only, but the spec treats `0-7` as a plain range that covers the whole week.

The day-of-week field counted as matching every day when it held only `NL` or `N#K` items, so `1#3` and `5L` matched any day. The spec says only `*` or `?` matches every day. The code also rejected `L` inside a list, turned `0-7` into Sunday only, and stripped whitespace inside quoted values in `parse_fields`, which its docstring says to keep.

Built the day-name table from `calendar.day_abbr`, which counts from Monday as 0, so `MON` meant Sunday, `THU` meant Wednesday and `SUN` meant Saturday. The spec numbers day of week 0 to 7 with 0 and 7 as Sunday and names `SUN`-`SAT`, so `MON` is 1 and `THU` is 4.

Built the day name table from `calendar.day_abbr`, which counts from Monday, so `MON` became 0 and every day name meant the day before it. The spec numbers the day-of-week field with 0 and 7 as Sunday, so `MON` must be 1 and `SUN` must be 0.

The parser rejects any item containing the letter `L` before it looks up names, so the month name `JUL` raises `ValueError` as an invalid special item. The spec allows `JAN` to `DEC` in the month field, so `JUL` should mean July and the expression should match.

When `after` fell exactly on a minute, `next_run` tried that same minute first, rejected it as not strictly later, and then skipped to the next day instead of trying the next minute. SCHEDULE.md says the result is the first run strictly after `after`, and gives the example that a schedule running every minute goes from 10:00:00 to 10:01, but the code returns the next midnight.

The parser rejects any item containing the letter `L` as a misplaced last day marker before it looks up names, so the month name `JUL` raises `ValueError`. The spec allows month names `JAN` to `DEC` in any case, so `JUL` is a valid month and both expressions are valid.

Read `1/3` in the day-of-week field as Monday and Thursday only, because `N/S` was built with `range(N % 7, 7)` and stopped at 6. The spec says `N/S` lists N up to the field's maximum, and day of week goes up to 7, which is Sunday, so Sunday counts too.

The code read `N/S` in the day-of-week field as running only up to 6, so `1/3` gave Monday and Thursday only. The spec says `N/S` runs up to the field's maximum, which is 7 for day of week, so `1/3` also includes 7, which is Sunday.
